Created by `CreateDocumentTypeFolders`. Sort every new document type into one of them: - **Page** — a document that renders. May use compositions. - **Block** — element for block list/grid. Renders. Never used as a composition. - **Composition** — element only composed onto others. Never rendered, never pickable. Never put real content behind a composition (removing a composition permanently deletes its content). - **Data** — element that never renders (settings, events, people). - **Repository** — document that never renders; a container/root node. The content root is always a Repository. - **Repository Item** — document that never renders; the pickable records inside a Repository. 2. **The content root is a Repository**: `siteRoot` (in the Repositories folder) is the only allowed root type; a published "WWW" node is created on first boot. Add sites as Pages beneath it — you are multi-site ready by default. - **Give the site Page a domain, or nothing answers on `/`.** WWW never renders, so the first real page is a child and Umbraco routes it under its node name (`/blog/`) until a domain says otherwise. For a single site, assign it the domain `/`; for several, give each its own hostname. Over MCP that is one call: `put-document-domains` with `{ "defaultIsoCode": "en-US", "domains": [{ "domainName": "/", "isoCode": "en-US" }] }`. 3. **Data types are never at the folder root**: `DataTypeSavedHandler` (in `Notifications/`) moves every data type saved at root into `/Umbraco/` (built-in) or `/Custom/` (yours). The migration organizes the shipped ones on first boot. 4. **Compose in `Composers/`, not Program.cs.** Program.cs stays as scaffolded; non-Umbraco concerns go in `WebApplicationBuilder` extension methods. 5. **Production runs in production mode**: `appsettings.json` is Production (models Nothing, UseHttps, no template editing); `appsettings.Development.json` is where development conveniences live. 6. **Aliases are English camelCase.** Translation keys are PascalCase dot-separated (`My.Dictionary.Item`); folders have no values themselves. Media lives in folders. 7. **uSync everything** (installed, version matched to the Umbraco major). On Umbraco Cloud use Umbraco Deploy instead. ## ModelsBuilder SourceCodeAuto in development. Generated models land in `Umbraco.Bench.Umbraco/Models/ModelsBuilder/` with namespace `Umbraco.Bench.Umbraco.Models`. Never edit generated files; extend via partials next to them. **When you change schema over MCP, generated models hit the disk immediately but the running site is still on the old assembly.** So work in this order: 1. **Model** — document types, element types, data types, templates, allowed children. 2. **Content** — create and publish. input.name: MCP Is the USB-C Port for AI

values.value: Before MCP, every AI integration was a bespoke cable. The Model Context Protocol gives assistants one standard plug — and that changes everything about how tools get connected.
MCP Is the USB-C Port for AI
One plug, every tool: why a boring standard is the most exciting thing to happen to AI assistants.

value.markup:
Remember the drawer full of chargers? A different cable for every phone, camera and laptop. That is what AI integrations looked like until recently. Every assistant needed its own custom connector for every tool: one plugin format here, a bespoke function-calling schema there, a pile of glue code in between. With M models and N tools you needed M × N integrations, and most of them were never built.

One protocol, both directions

The Model Context Protocol (MCP) is an open standard for connecting AI applications to the systems where data and actions live. A tool exposes itself once, as an MCP server. Any MCP-capable client — a chat app, an IDE, a coding agent — can then discover and use it. M × N becomes M + N.

A server describes three kinds of things:

  • Tools — actions the model can take, each with a JSON schema for its input.

  • Resources — data the model can read, addressed by URI.

  • Prompts — reusable, parameterised templates a user can invoke.

values.value: The best standards are boring. Nobody gets excited about a plug — they get excited about everything they can finally connect.
A shape that fits every slot. Photo: Edge2Edge Media / Unsplash

value.markup:
Why this matters

Build once, work everywhere. A vendor ships one MCP server, and it works in every compatible assistant. You don't need a separate plugin for each one.

Discovery is built in. Clients ask a server what it can do at runtime. Nobody hard-codes tool lists, so new capabilities show up without touching the client.

Local by default. A server can run as a plain process on your machine over stdio. Your credentials and data stay where they already are.

The network effect kicks in

Every new MCP server makes every MCP client more useful, and every new client makes every server more valuable. That flywheel is why the ecosystem grew so fast. Databases, ticket trackers, design tools, browsers, and yes, content management systems like Umbraco, can all join the conversation.

USB-C didn't make laptops faster. It made them easier to connect, and that turned out to matter more. MCP does the same for AI: it doesn't make the model smarter, but it gives the model far more to work with.

input.name: This Blog Was Built Through MCP

values.value: Document types, block grids, media and these very words were all created by an AI agent talking to Umbraco over MCP. Here's what that looks like, and why it beats clicking.
This Blog Was Built Through MCP
No clicking through the backoffice. An agent, a CMS and a protocol in between.

value.markup:
Every page on this site came out of a conversation. An AI agent connected to the Umbraco MCP server, read the project's conventions, and then did the work: it created the element types and block grid data types, filed them in the right folders, imported the photos into the media library, and wrote and published the posts you're reading.

What the agent actually did

  1. Content modeling. It created five block element types (hero, rich text, image, quote and blog post list), two block grid data types, and the Blog Front Page and Blog Post page types, each with a template.

  2. Media. It imported Unsplash photos from a local folder straight into a Blog media folder.

  3. Content. It composed each page as a block grid value and published it, then read the document back to check the structure took.

  4. Routing. It assigned the blog a domain so it answers on /.

values.value: The developer's desk, minus most of the clicking. Photo: Christopher Gower / Unsplash
The interesting part isn't that the AI can write a blog post. It's that it can put the post in the right place, in the right shape, following your rules.

value.markup:
Why this is awesome

Structure, not just text. A chatbot that writes copy still leaves you to paste it in. An agent with MCP works with the CMS's real model: document types, block grids, media pickers. What it produces is proper structured content that editors can keep working on in the backoffice.

Conventions are respected. Because the agent goes through the same management API as the backoffice, the CMS's own rules still apply. Here, data types end up in the right folders, uSync exports every change, and nothing bypasses validation.

It is all local. The MCP server runs next to the site on a developer machine. It uses a dedicated API user that only exists in development, and it can only read media from an allow-listed folder.

Tedious becomes conversational. “Add a quote block to the post grid.” “Import these ten photos into a folder.” “Publish everything under Blog.” These used to take dozens of clicks each. Now they take one sentence.

MCP doesn't replace editors or developers. It removes the busywork between having an idea and seeing it on the page.

values.value: MCP Is the USB-C Port for AI
One plug, every tool: why a boring standard is the most exciting thing to happen to AI assistants.

value.markup:
Remember the drawer full of chargers? A different cable for every phone, camera and laptop. That is what AI integrations looked like until recently. Every assistant needed its own custom connector for every tool: one plugin format here, a bespoke function-calling schema there, a pile of glue code in between. With M models and N tools you needed M × N integrations, and most of them were never built.

One protocol, both directions

The Model Context Protocol (MCP) is an open standard for connecting AI applications to the systems where data and actions live. A tool exposes itself once, as an MCP server. Any MCP-capable client — a chat app, an IDE, a coding agent — can then discover and use it. M × N becomes M + N.

A server describes three kinds of things:

  • Tools — actions the model can take, each with a JSON schema for its input.

  • Resources — data the model can read, addressed by URI.

  • Prompts — reusable, parameterised templates a user can invoke.

value.markup:
Why this matters

Build once, work everywhere. A vendor ships one MCP server, and it works in every compatible assistant. You don't need a separate plugin for each one.

Discovery is built in. Clients ask a server what it can do at runtime. Nobody hard-codes tool lists, so new capabilities show up without touching the client.

Local by default. A server can run as a plain process on your machine over stdio. Your credentials and data stay where they already are.

The network effect kicks in

Every new MCP server makes every MCP client more useful, and every new client makes every server more valuable. That flywheel is why the ecosystem grew so fast. Databases, ticket trackers, design tools, browsers, and yes, content management systems like Umbraco, can all join the conversation.

USB-C didn't make laptops faster. It made them easier to connect, and that turned out to matter more. MCP does the same for AI: it doesn't make the model smarter, but it gives the model far more to work with.

// Commandment 3: a custom data type can never be at the root of the data type folder.
// Built-in data types are grouped under /Umbraco/<editorAlias>, custom ones under /Custom/<editorAlias>.
public class DataTypeOrganizationService(
    IDataTypeService dataTypeService,
    IDataTypeContainerService containerService)
{
    private const string CustomFolderName = "Custom";
    private const string BuiltInFolderName = "Umbraco";

    public async Task<int> OrganizeAllAsync()
    {
        var all = await dataTypeService.GetAllAsync();
        var organized = 0;
        foreach (var dataType in all.Where(dt => dt.ParentId == -1))
        {
            if (await OrganizeAsync(dataType))
                organized++;
        }

        return organized;
    }

    public async Task<bool> OrganizeAsync(IDataType dataType)
    {
        if (dataType.ParentId != -1)

content.text:
The blog is up and running at **https://localhost:44317/**. The front page lists both posts, and all three pages return 200 with every block rendering (none fall back to "Could not render component"). I created all content types, media and content through the MCP server, with no migrations, and uSync exported the changes to `uSync/v18/`. I didn't open the site in a browser, so I've only checked the HTML and image URLs, not how it looks.

**How to view it**
- Front page: https://localhost:44317/ — it has the domain `/`, so it answers at the root.
- Post 1: https://localhost:44317/mcp-is-the-usb-c-port-for-ai/
- Post 2: https://localhost:44317/this-blog-was-built-through-mcp/
- Backoffice: https://localhost:44317/umbraco (admin@example.com / 1234567890)

Umbraco is still running in the background from my session.

**What I built**
- **Blocks** (in the Blocks folder): `heroBlock`, `richTextBlock`, `imageBlock`, `quoteBlock` and `blogPostListBlock`. The post list shows the blog's posts newest first, with an optional maximum.
- **Block grids:** two 12-column grids, *Blog Front Page Grid* and *Blog Post Grid*. They were filed under `/Custom/Umbraco.BlockGrid` automatically.
- **Pages** (in the Pages folder):
  - `blogFrontPage` sits under WWW and only allows posts as children. I updated the site root type to allow it.
  - `blogPost` has the block grid plus *Publish Date*, *Excerpt* and *Teaser Image* on a Listing tab, which the front-page list uses.
  - Each page type has its own template, both sharing a `layout` template.
- **Media:** six Unsplash photos imported into a *Blog* media folder, each credited to its photographer.
- **Content:** the *Blog* front page (hero plus post list) and two posts, built from hero, rich text, quote and image blocks:
  - "MCP Is the USB-C Port for AI" — includes a half-width image next to half-width text.
  - "This Blog Was Built Through MCP"
- **Razor:** done after a stop, build and restart, following the block pipeline in AGENTS.md:
  - One adapter per block in `Views/Partials/blockgrid/Components/<alias>.cshtml`.
  - Plain view models in `Models/Blocks/`.
  - One ViewComponent per block in `ViewComponents/`.
  - All markup in `Views/Shared/Components/<Name>/Default.cshtml`.
  - Pages render their blocks with `GetBlockGridHtmlAsync`.
- **Styling:** Tailwind. I added CSS for the block grid layout and rich text to `Umbraco.Bench.Frontend/src/site.css` and ran the frontend build.

**Problems and things to know**
- **Focal points from the MCP import:** `create-media-multiple` gave every image a focal point of `{left: 0, top: 0.5}`, so every crop was pinned to the left edge. I re-centered all six through MCP with `update-media`. Watch for this on future imports.
- **Node in Git Bash:** the shell profile doesn't set up `fnm`, so `npm` only worked from PowerShell. Rebuild the CSS there with `fnm env --shell powershell | Out-String | Invoke-Expression`, then `npm run build` in the Frontend folder.
- **Small changes to existing files:**
  - I added the project's model and block-model namespaces to `Views/_ViewImports.cshtml`.
  - I put the ViewComponent classes in a new `ViewComponents/` folder, since AGENTS.md doesn't say where they belong.
- **Not built:**
  - No block settings (spacing, background, anchor) and no block grid areas.
  - The *Publish Date* shown on posts is a manual field, separate from Umbraco's own publish date.
